did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a title attributing it to Moses, who is called “the man of God,” and presents the Lord as a “dwelling place”—a place of refuge and sustenance—for every generation.

Did you know? The Lord’s greatness is described in relation to the time of creation: he existed before the mountains were born and before the earth and the world were formed, and his existence continues “from everlasting to everlasting.”

Did you know? The psalm compares a thousand years in the Lord’s sight to a day that has passed, and even to a night watch, highlighting the difference between human perceptions of time and the Lord’s eternity.
Did you know? Human life is described as something that quickly flows away and as a sleep; in the morning, it is compared to grass—a picture of something that appears briefly and then disappears.
Did you know? The psalm speaks of a life expectancy of seventy years, or eighty if one is strong, but adds that even those years are filled with toil and a sense of passing away.
Did you know? Recognizing how short life is, the psalm asks to “number our days”—to understand the limits of time—in order to gain “a heart of wisdom.”
Did you know? In its final section, the psalm shifts from describing life’s brevity to making a direct appeal to the Lord: “Return, Lord,” asking for mercy and comfort for his servants.
Did you know? The request “Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love” connects the morning with the possibility of renewal, joy, and singing after a time of suffering.

Did you know? The psalm asks that the Lord’s work be seen by his servants, and that the next generation also see his glory, creating a link between generations and between human experience and the Lord’s work.
Did you know? The conclusion asks not merely for momentary success, but for the Lord to establish and sustain the work of human hands: “Yes, establish the work of our hands.”
